name: Dirty Green
lede: Dirty Green is a muted, yellowish reading of [[green]], settled on by the crowd-sourced 2010 xkcd color survey.

sections.title: A plain modifier for a muddied hue
sections.body:
The name follows a plain modifier grammar, *dirty* plus [[green]], meaning duller and more yellowed than the plain color; it comes from the xkcd online color survey of 2010 rather than any historical dictionary or plate [1]. Our library also records the exact same hex under the separate name Moss Olive, a duplicate entry from another source [1].

Its closest look-alike on file is [[khaki-green]], about 3.6 units off, with [[military-green]] and [[muddy-green]] a little further out [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 0.31% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (74 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 47 [3]. In our archive it is rarer than 51% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.6% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (10 paintings), 2.6 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent across its 47 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. It is painted most often by John Singer Sargent (4 of 287 works here); no painter stands out against the museums' baseline [3]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.2x expected (19 of 3,443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1513, 497 years before the name's 2010 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
